message:
QUESTION:
Did the 1 June move to a new content delivery network (CDN) improve the site's conversion rate, and what is a faster site worth?

DATA:
An online retailer migrated its website to a new content delivery network (CDN) on 1 June. Two weeks before (18-31 May) vs two weeks after (1-14 June):

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June |
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 |
| Median page load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s |
| 95th-percentile page load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% |

Conversion = orders / sessions. Page load times come from real-user monitoring across all page views.

Same two calendar periods last year, when there were no site or infrastructure changes: conversion 2.4% (18-31 May) and 2.6% (1-14 June).

The retailer's conversion rate rises every year in early June when the summer ranges launch. This year the summer ranges again launched on 1 June. No other site changes were made between 18 May and 14 June.

KNOWN FLAWS:
F1. [calculation] The reduction is (7.5 − 4.8) / 7.5 = 36%. 56% comes from dividing the 2.7 s fall by the new value (4.8). The draft's claim that the slowest experiences 'improved even more' than the median (34%) is barely true at 36%. CORRECTION: 95th percentile fell by 36%, similar to the median's 34%.
F2. [misreport] The data show bounce rate fell from 48% to 44%. CORRECTION: A 4-point (8% relative) fall in bounce rate.
F3. [method] Ignores the seasonal baseline: the same calendar periods last year, with no site changes, show the same 0.2-point rise (2.4% to 2.6%) from the summer range launch, which happened again on 1 June. CORRECTION: Year-over-year difference-in-differences: (2.70 − 2.50) − (2.6 − 2.4) = 0.0 points. There is no detectable conversion effect of the CDN.
F4. [inference] Derives a linear causal 'value per second' from one confounded before/after comparison and extrapolates it beyond the observed range. CORRECTION: The data support no value-per-second estimate (the seasonally adjusted effect is about zero). A randomised latency experiment would be needed.

EXTENSIONS:
- Run a statistical check on the raw conversion change (2.50% vs 2.70%, z of about 4) and contrast it with the seasonally adjusted comparison, showing that a highly significant before/after change can be entirely seasonal.
- Check whether the sessions increase (+5%) is also seasonal, using last year's session counts for the same periods, which the analyst should request.
- Segment by device or connection type: speed gains typically matter most on mobile and slow connections, so an effect masked in the aggregate could appear there (data would be needed).

FINAL VERSION:
# CDN migration: performance and conversion impact

## Summary

- **The 1 June CDN migration made the site much faster.** Median load time fell 34% and 95th-percentile load time fell 36%. The CDN can reasonably be credited with this gain.
- **We found no evidence that the migration raised conversion.** Conversion rose from 2.50% to 2.70%. Over the same two weeks last year, with no site changes, it rose by the same amount, from 2.4% to 2.6%. Both years had the early-June summer-range launch. The result is the same whether the seasonal rise is measured in points or in percentages.
- **That does not mean the CDN had no effect.** The comparison is too imprecise to tell. Our best estimate of the CDN's effect is about zero.
  - Rounding and sampling noise alone give a 95% range of about **±0.16 points**.
  - That range leaves out year-to-year variation in the seasonal rise, which one prior year cannot measure. The true uncertainty is therefore wider. **±0.25 points** is a reasonable working allowance.
  - Either range includes effects large enough to be commercially worthwhile.
- **We can't yet say what a faster site is worth.** A reliable figure needs:
  - unrounded prior-year data
  - a comparison of traffic and revenue, not just conversion
  - ideally, a controlled test, which would take about 8 weeks with traffic split 50/50.

## Background

- The site moved to a new CDN on 1 June. This note compares the two weeks before (18–31 May) with the two weeks after (1–14 June).
- Load times come from real-user monitoring (RUM) across all page views, so they reflect what customers actually experienced.
- The figures are site-wide totals. They do not include device, channel, revenue or average order value.
- No other site changes were made between 18 May and 14 June.
- The summer ranges launched on 1 June, as they do every year, and conversion always rises in early June. Both changes happened on the same day, which is the main obstacle to measuring the CDN's effect.

## Speed

| Metric | 18–31 May | 1–14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s | −1.1 s (−34%) |
| 95th-percentile load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s | −2.7 s (−36%) |

- **The improvement is large and broad.** Both typical and slow page loads became about a third faster. The slowest loads saved the most time in absolute terms (2.7 s).
- **A seasonal cause is very unlikely.** Higher summer traffic and heavier new-range pages would, if anything, slow the site. The CDN's true gain may therefore be slightly understated.
- **One caveat about the page mix.** RUM covers all page views. Lower bounce means visitors viewed a somewhat different mix of pages after the change. This affects the comparison slightly but does not change the conclusion.

## Traffic and engagement

| Metric | 18–31 May | 1–14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 | +5% |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 | +13% |
| Orders per day | ~357 | 405 | +13% |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% | −4 pts (−8% relative) |

- Every metric moved in the direction a faster site would produce.
- The summer launch would also likely lift every one of them.
- We don't have last year's sessions, orders or bounce rate for these periods, so we can't separate the two causes for any of these metrics.

## Conversion

| | 18–31 May | 1–14 June | Change (points) | Change (relative) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| This year (CDN migration + summer launch) | 2.50% | 2.70% | +0.20 | +8.0% |
| Last year (summer launch only) | 2.4% | 2.6% | +0.2 | +8.3% |
| **Estimated CDN effect** | | | **≈ 0** | **≈ −0.3%** |

**Why the simple comparison misleads.** A before/after comparison would credit the CDN with +0.2 points, or about 420 extra orders a fortnight. Yet the same rise happened last year with no site changes. Subtracting last year's seasonal rise leaves a central estimate of about zero.

**The result holds on a relative scale.** The adjustment above assumes the summer launch adds the same number of points each year. The lift might instead scale with the baseline. Applying last year's +8.3% relative lift to this year's 2.50% predicts 2.71% with no CDN effect. The actual figure was 2.70%, so the conclusion is unchanged.

Three things make the estimate uncertain.

### 1. Last year's figures are rounded
The figures 2.4% and 2.6% are given to one decimal place. Last year's true seasonal rise could therefore be anywhere from 0.10 to 0.30 points.

- If last year was really 2.45% → 2.55%, the seasonal rise was 0.1 points. The CDN would then account for about 0.1 points, half of this year's rise.
- If last year was really 2.35% → 2.65%, the seasonal rise was 0.3 points. The CDN effect would then look about 0.1 points negative.
- These extremes are unlikely. If each rounded figure could be anywhere within ±0.05, the rounding error in the difference follows a triangular distribution on ±0.10, with a standard deviation of about 0.04 points.

### 2. Sampling noise
- Each two-week conversion rate has a standard error of about 0.035 points.
- The comparison combines four rates, two from each year. Assuming last year had similar volumes, the combined standard error is about 0.07 points, or **±0.14 points** at 95% confidence.
- This is a lower bound. It treats sessions as independent, but repeat visitors and multiple sessions per buyer add more noise.

### 3. The seasonal rise varies from year to year
With only one prior year, we can't estimate how much the early-June lift varies. Any variation adds uncertainty on top of points 1 and 2.

### Combined uncertainty
- **Rounding and sampling combined** (standard deviations of about 0.04 and 0.07) give a 95% range of about **±0.16 points**.
  - Simply adding the two ranges (±0.10 + ±0.14 ≈ ±0.24) would overstate the spread, because both extremes are unlikely to occur together.
- **The ±0.16 leaves out year-to-year variation in the seasonal rise**, because we cannot measure it. The true uncertainty is therefore wider.
- **As a working figure, ±0.25 points** (roughly ±10% relative) is a reasonable allowance. It is a judgement, not a calculation.

### Comparison with industry figures
- A commonly quoted rule of thumb says each second saved raises conversion by roughly 2–7%. Treat this as an assumption, not a sourced estimate. Published figures vary widely and are often poorly controlled.
- For a 1.1-second gain at a 2.5% baseline, that rule implies about 0.05–0.2 points.
- That range lies entirely inside our uncertainty, so our data can neither confirm nor rule it out.

**Conclusion on conversion:** the data give no evidence that the CDN raised conversion. They also cannot rule out a commercially meaningful effect.

## Conversion rate may not capture the CDN's full value

- **Traffic.**
  - Sessions rose 5%. A faster site can attract more sessions, for example through better search ranking or fewer abandoned visits.
  - If the CDN brought in extra, lower-intent sessions, they would add orders while *diluting* the conversion rate.
- **Measurement.**
  - With a 7.5-second 95th percentile before the migration, some visitors may have left before the analytics tag fired and were never counted.
  - A faster site would record more of these visitors. This would inflate sessions and could mask a real conversion gain.
  - However, newly recorded visitors would mostly be bounces, which should have pushed the bounce rate *up*. Instead, it fell from 48% to 44%.
  - So either this effect is small, or the underlying improvement in engagement is larger than the headline figures show. Treat this as something to check, not a likely explanation.
- **Revenue.**
  - "What is a faster site worth" is ultimately a revenue question.
  - These data contain no average order value or revenue. Faster pages could change basket size as well as the number of orders.

So the right comparison is growth in sessions, orders and revenue against the same periods last year, not the conversion rate alone.

## What is a faster site worth?

**These data can't answer this.**

**Why the naive estimate fails.** Dividing this year's 0.2-point conversion rise by the 1.1-second improvement in median load time gives about 0.18 points per second. That figure has two problems:
- It attributes the whole seasonal rise to the CDN.
- It assumes conversion responds in a straight line to load time, which may not hold outside the range we observed.

Do not use it in business cases.

**What is at stake.** At 200,000–210,000 sessions per fortnight (the May and June levels), each 0.1 points of conversion is worth about **200–210 orders a fortnight**. If traffic stayed at that level all year, that would be roughly **5,200–5,500 orders a year**. June traffic is seasonally high, so check annual traffic before relying on the upper figure. Multiply by average order value and margin to get a money figure.

This sizing has two uses:
- It sets a threshold for judging any future estimate.
- It shows that effects too small for this comparison to detect could still be worth having.

## Next steps

1. **Get unrounded prior-year data.**
   - Request last year's exact conversion, sessions, orders, revenue and bounce rate for both periods.
   - This removes the rounding uncertainty at no cost and is the quickest way to narrow the estimate.
2. **Compare volumes and revenue against last year, not just conversion.**
   - Check whether this year's growth in sessions, orders and revenue exceeds last year's seasonal growth.
3. **Strengthen the seasonal baseline.**
   - Repeat the comparison using several prior years and daily data.
   - This shows how much the early-June lift normally varies, and therefore how large a CDN effect we could detect.
4. **Look for a dose-response pattern.**
   - Split the data by device, region and connection type, comparing each segment with the same segment last year.
   - If conversion rose more where load times improved most, that is evidence of a real speed effect.
5. **Run a controlled test if a precise value is needed.**
   - Options include routing a randomised share of traffic through the old delivery path, if it is still available, or adding latency to a random share of sessions. Plan for three issues:
   - **Sample size and duration.**
     - Detecting a 0.1-point effect at a 2.5% baseline needs about 390,000 sessions per group, or about 780,000 in total. This assumes 5% two-sided significance and 80% power.
     - At about 105,000 sessions a week, a 50/50 split takes **about 8 weeks**.
     - A 10% exposed share would need about 2.2 million sessions in total, roughly **21 weeks**.
     - Non-independent sessions would lengthen both.
     - Agree the minimum effect worth detecting (see the sizing above) before designing the test.
   - **Revenue cost.**
     - Slowing the site for some customers will cost some sales.
     - Weigh this against the longer duration a small exposed share requires.
   - **Asymmetry.**
     - Customers may react more strongly to a site getting slower than to one getting faster, so adding latency may overstate the value of speed.
     - Testing a larger delay finishes sooner but assumes the effect scales with the delay. State both assumptions alongside any result.
6. **Keep monitoring load times** through the summer to confirm the speed gain holds as traffic grows.
7. **Don't use conversion uplift to justify further speed work until steps 1–5 give a credible estimate.**
   - Performance work may still be justified on other grounds, such as user experience, search ranking or infrastructure cost.

## Conclusion

- **The CDN made the site clearly faster.** Median load time fell 34% and 95th-percentile load time fell 36%.
- **There is no evidence it raised conversion.** Conversion rose 0.2 points, but last year's seasonal rise was the same size, whether measured in points or percentages.
- **A meaningful effect cannot be ruled out.**
  - Rounding and sampling noise alone leave a range of about ±0.16 points.
  - Year-to-year variation in the seasonal rise widens it further, to roughly ±0.25 points as a working allowance.
- **Before valuing speed:**
  - Get unrounded prior-year data.
  - Compare traffic and revenue as well as conversion.
  - For a reliable figure, run a controlled test of about 8 weeks instead of a before/after comparison that overlaps the summer launch.

---

*Changes from the draft:* I rechecked all figures and they hold. The only correction is the duration for a 10% exposed share: it is about 21 weeks (2.17 million sessions at 105,000 a week), not 20. I also clarified that the 8-week estimate assumes a 50/50 split and tightened some wording.
